sources.title: Wide Wide West: The Hateful Eight

items.title: Chilling a Hollywood soundstage to 30°F so you can see The Hateful Eight's breath
items.body: Quentin Tarantino's production moved the set of Minnie's Haberdashery off a Colorado location and onto a soundstage at Red Studios Hollywood, then chilled that stage to 30° Fahrenheit and 80 percent humidity — the point being to make the cast's exhaled breath visible on camera, according to American Cinematographer's set report. The same shoot used Ultra Panavision 70, the 2.76:1 widescreen format that had gone almost 50 years without a feature, and which Tarantino calls the widest format there is outside three-screen Cinerama. The movie's coldness is partly a photographic problem solved with HVAC: winter as a controlled studio condition rather than weather you have to chase.

sources.title: Ceres Facts

items.title: Ceres is the asteroid belt's biggest object — and a quarter of its mass
items.body: Dwarf planet Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter and the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system, NASA notes. It is also a useful exercise in scale: Ceres accounts for 25 percent of the asteroid belt's total mass, which tells you how little the rest of that crowded-looking region adds up to. The comparison cuts the other way too — Pluto is still 14 times more massive than Ceres. Largest in the belt does not mean large.

sources.title: Edie Falco: ‘Alcohol was the answer to all my problems – and the cause of them’

discussion.body: Carmela's self-deception isn't ignorance so much as upkeep. She knows the money has a source and keeps choosing not to follow it, which is harder work than not knowing would be.

Fair, but that reading risks turning it into a character defect rather than an acting problem. The Guardian's claim is about the performance: it's Falco's sincerity that makes the self-deception readable as a gap instead of a buried fact.
It also gives the show a neat division of labour. Carmela says the true thing out loud about the mistresses, which makes her silence about the money look like a decision rather than a blind spot.

items.title: Why Edie Falco's ordinariness makes Carmela's self-deception land
items.body: The Guardian's profile of Edie Falco makes a specific argument about why she is so good at a certain kind of role: her air of straightforwardness and relatability is what makes her performances of self-deceiving characters land. The Carmela example is the clean one. As the mob wife in The Sopranos, she could tell Tony what she thought of him staying out all night with his mistresses, but she could not admit to herself that he does much worse to fund the life she loves. The performance works because the gap isn't hidden from us — it's right there on a face we instinctively trust. The same profile notes the pattern repeating with Nurse Jackie, where a scrubbed-clean look sat on top of a drug addiction.

sources.title: Calgary council divided on whether city should take official stance on Alberta separatism

items.title: Calgary council split over taking a stance on Alberta's independence referendum
items.body: Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas says he anticipates bringing urgent business or calling a special meeting so city council can debate whether to take an official stance on the upcoming Alberta independence referendum this fall, CBC reports. Some councillors argue the debate sits outside their jurisdiction. That is the real question underneath the procedural one: whether a municipality has standing at all in a provincial separation vote, or whether taking a side would just be a council speaking for residents it has no mandate to bind.

sources.title: Rocket Report: China wants a Raptor 3 engine; SpaceX set for big Starship test

discussion.body: Worth noting the report frames ULA's decline alongside Avio's gain rather than as a SpaceX-only story. The pressure on expendable launch isn't monopoly, it's margin competition.
Describing the company as tied to an expendable rocket cuts both ways. If the rocket is the problem, the fix is a vehicle program, not a strategy memo — and that's a very different kind of hard.

items.title: The Beastie Boys sample buried in the Rust Belt: why ULA's rocket problem is a business-model problem
items.body:
United Launch Alliance was, as recently as a decade ago, a launch company that could claim dominance over the US industry — a joint venture co-owned by Boeing and Lockheed Martin. The company's fortunes have since faded fast, and the question now is what happens to a launch provider tied to an expendable rocket, according to Ars Technica's Rocket Report.

The contrast that makes the ULA story legible sits in the same roundup: Italian launch services provider Avio has seen an influx of customers who could not secure launch opportunities with SpaceX, European Spaceflight reports. That is the shape of the post-SpaceX market. Demand does not evaporate when one provider fills its manifest; it spills over to whoever can fly. Avio is catching it. ULA, whose vehicle is designed to be thrown away after one flight, is not positioned the same way.

The mechanism is simple enough to say plainly: a rocket you discard after each launch has to earn back its entire cost on that one flight. Reusability changes the arithmetic by spreading hardware cost across multiple flights — which is why a company whose future is described as tied to an expendable rocket faces a structural question, not just a scheduling one.

sources.title: The Free Rider Problem

discussion.body: The false-belief case is the one people skip past. If a group's members are simply wrong about what serves them, the fix might be information after all — which blurs the clean line the entry draws.
The distinction earns its keep precisely because it tells you whether to build a better map or rewrite the incentives. Most policy arguments conflate the two and then wonder why the memo didn't work.

items.title: Collective action problems vs. coordination problems: the difference is not information, it's interest
items.body:
A collective action problem is a situation where every member of a group would be better off if everyone did A than if no one did A — but the parties' conflicting views of their own interests risk producing an outcome worse for everyone than universal A. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry on the free rider problem states the definition carefully, because the careful version is where the interesting parts live.

The entry draws a sharp line between this and a coordination problem. In a coordination problem, a mutually advantageous outcome — the example given is meeting at a rendezvous point — can be obstructed by a lack of information rather than by conflicting interests. Two people who both want to meet but never named a place have a coordination problem. Two people who each want the other to show up first have a collective action problem. The remedy differs accordingly: publish the location, versus change the payoffs.

The definition is deliberately broad in ways worth noticing. It allows that a collective action problem can arise when everyone's interests genuinely are best served by doing A, yet many people falsely believe they are individually better off not doing A. It also allows different ways of specifying what counts as better or worse for an individual. And the entry notes one consequence of the coordination/collective-action distinction: it precludes identifying interests with preference-satisfaction. If interests were just whatever people prefer, the category of false belief about one's own interest would have nowhere to sit — and neither, arguably, would the problem.

sources.title: Hedge funds and bond market liquidity dynamics at the onset of the 2026 Middle East conflict

items.title: No evidence hedge funds drove Government of Canada bond illiquidity at the start of the 2026 Middle East war, Bank of Canada researchers find
items.body:
A Bank of Canada paper asks whether hedge funds contributed to illiquidity in the Government of Canada bond market at the onset of the Middle East war in early 2026. The researchers report they found no evidence that they did.

The supporting detail is about behavior rather than intentions: hedge funds remained active in primary auctions, and their secondary market trading stayed broadly consistent with their usual relative-value strategies. That is a specific finding about a specific market window, not a general verdict on hedge fund risk-taking.

sources.title: Finessing Killers of the Flower Moon at Company 3

discussion.body: This is a nice inversion of how grading is usually described. The craft isn't in what the toolset can do; it's in which subset you allow yourself before you start.
Printer points as a starting discipline only works because the LUTs already do the heavy lifting. The constraint is downstream of a decision made before the session begins.

items.title: How a colorist grades a film by pretending it's still 1990: printer points before windows and keys
items.body:
Yvan Lucas, who worked on the color grade for Killers of the Flower Moon, describes a workflow in American Cinematographer that is essentially an act of deliberate self-constraint. He spent years as a timer in Paris at Éclair, where cinematographers chose film stock and the timer contributed through printer lights. When he moved into color grading, with its lift, gamma, gain and far more, he kept working the way he had as a timer.

The method: build custom LUTs that function much like custom film stocks, then begin by using only printer points inside Baselight, because that retains the qualities of a film finish. His stated reason is that printer points do not affect contrast or add windows or keys. All of that can be done later. He prefers to do a great deal of the work upfront in the LUTs.

Lucas says Rodrigo Prieto likes to work the same way, and that the two think similarly about color for films — which is why Prieto has wanted to work with him over the years. The interesting bit isn't nostalgia. It's that a digital grading suite contains every tool needed to make a shot look synthetic, and the discipline is in choosing the smaller set first.

sources.title: “I realised any attempt to replicate is going to be a failure”: Sophy Romvari on Blue Heron

discussion.body: The containment image is the whole first half: a world you can see entirely and touch not at all. Withholding the conversations, the behaviours, the tragedy is the same bargain — you're given the view but denied the access.

Then the film reverses it. Sending adult Sasha back with a camera and a documentary project is a refusal to stay outside the dome; the magic return is the opposite of observation from a safe distance.

items.title: Blue Heron builds a snow globe, then walks back inside it
items.body: Sophy Romvari's semi-autobiographical debut plays like the object the BFI reaches for: a snow globe, unhurried and nostalgic, a self-contained world you observe as if through a glass dome. The world is a Hungarian-Canadian family undone by a disruptive son and by the systems that fail him, and the film is precise about what it withholds — conversations you never hear, behaviours you never understand, a tragedy you never see. What makes the withholding bearable is the intimacy of eight-year-old Sasha (Eylul Guven), whose late-1990s summer of balmy boredom is disrupted by her teenage brother Jeremy's increasingly destructive behaviour. His patient but exasperated parents (Ádám Tompa and Iringó Réti) seek help from various professionals and rarely feel heard. Then Romvari lifts the dome off entirely: adult Sasha (Amy Zimmer) is a filmmaker making a documentary to process her hazy memories of Jeremy, searching for the answers her parents searched for years earlier. A moment of magic returns her to them and to her childhood home, and the film becomes a meditation on the inability to alter the past. A snow globe is a world you can see all of and touch none of; the second half is what happens when someone decides to try touching it anyway.

sources.title: David Hume

items.title: Hume wrote the Treatise at 23 and called it 'deadborn from the press'
items.body: In 1734, David Hume moved to La Flèche in France and, at twenty-three, began writing A Treatise of Human Nature. His verdict on how it landed became one of the more quotable lines in the history of philosophy: the book, he declared, fell 'deadborn from the press.' The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy treats that as an exaggeration — but only partly. The Treatise, it reports, certainly did far less spectacularly than Hume was hoping. There is something bracing in the mismatch: the work is now filed among the most consequential in its field, and its author spent his early twenties in another country writing it while convinced, briefly, that nobody had noticed.

sources.title: Automation and Inequality: How Robots Shift Income Between Workers and Owners

discussion.body: The labor share of value added is a firm-level ratio, not a statement about fairness. A ratio can hold steady while the composition of the labour income inside it changes — which is roughly why the paper bothers to flag the owner-income line.
And the scope matters: the finding is about direct effects within Canadian private corporations. It isn't a verdict on workers at suppliers, on the public sector, or on other countries.

items.title: What robot adoption did to Canadian payrolls — and what the labor share hides
items.body: A Bank of Canada paper examines the direct effects of industrial robot adoption on workers and owners inside Canadian private corporations, and its headline finding is not the one the usual robot story predicts. Adoption increases firm scale and per-worker payroll, the authors find, but it does not decrease the labor share of value added. That sounds like a clean rebuttal of the robots-take-labor's-cut narrative. The paper's wrinkle is accounting: labor income earned by owners, counted conventionally, masks the impact on non-owner workers. In other words, a stable-looking share can be stable for reasons that have nothing to do with how the gains are distributed among the people actually working there.

sources.title: 'Shadow surge' pushes immigration arrests to highs as Trump administration shifts tactics

items.title: Federal immigration enforcement leans on state and local police
items.body: Less than a year ago, aggressive immigration raids were drawing headlines and sparking protests, PBS reports. Recently, it says, the Trump administration has shifted its approach: rather than relying as heavily on high-profile operations, federal immigration authorities are working with state and local police. Geoff Bennett discussed the change with Lauren Villagran of The Marshall Project, who framed it as a 'shadow surge.' The practical question a quieter enforcement strategy raises is the harder one to answer — when the visible raids stop making news, what becomes of the scrutiny that came with them?

sources.title: Trump administration begins building border wall in Big Bend region of Texas

items.title: Construction begins on a $46 billion border wall plan
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports that construction has started on border wall work, which it calls an important milestone in the administration's $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology. The network frames the build as an effort to make good on a key Trump campaign promise to finish the wall. What the report does not offer is any accounting of how much of the barrier is already complete or how the $46 billion is broken down across walls, roads and surveillance technology — the milestone as reported is the start of building, not the completion of it.

sources.title: Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?

items.title: The Houthis are climbing Iran's "axis of resistance" rankings
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that after Houthi victories in Yemen, the group's importance in the US-Iran war has grown. In Iran's so-called "axis of resistance," Lebanon's Hezbollah had long been considered the most significant member; the Houthis, DW says, are now rising toward the top of that hierarchy. The shift is a repositioning of standing within an alliance rather than a formal transfer of command — the kind of change that matters most when the question is which partner can actually do something for Tehran, and which one is being asked to.

sources.title: Former Saskatoon Christian school principal found guilty of assaulting 3 students with paddle

items.title: Saskatoon jury convicts former Christian school principal on three assault counts
items.body: CBC reports that a Saskatoon jury found Duff Arthur Friesen, 68, the former principal of a private Christian school, guilty on three counts of assault. He had been accused of assaulting five former students with a weapon — a wooden paddle. The verdict resolves the charges at trial; the number of counts he was convicted on is lower than the number of alleged victims in the accusation CBC describes.

sources.title: What’s Queer About The Legend of Zelda?

discussion.body: The interesting move here is that nothing needs to be depicted for the reading to work. A romance that's set up and can never resolve is a structural fact about the story, not a hidden scene.

Or Link simply never grows up because he's a recurring mascot in games about dungeons — a commercial convenience that happens to be suggestive. A blocked romance and a deliberately queer one aren't the same claim.

Pugh's argument doesn't require intent. He's reading the effect of the pattern across a set of games with conventionally heteronormative plots, and if subversive potential only counted when it was obvious, it wouldn't be subversive.

items.title: Why a hero who never grows up can read as queer
items.body:
The subtext in Nintendo games, argues Tison Pugh in the Journal of Narrative Theory, emerges precisely where the surface looks most conventional. His case, summarized by JSTOR Daily: despite plots that are overarchingly heteronormative — male heroes rescuing imprisoned maidens — subversive potential shows up in numerous Nintendo titles anyway.

The Legend of Zelda is his central example, and the mechanism he identifies is the romance that cannot land. Link's perpetual childhood, Pugh writes, keeps him in a presexual world, and the story keeps constructing a romance storyline that can never be successfully navigated. The queerness he describes isn't a romance between two characters; it's a courtship structure built into the narrative and then made permanently unfulfillable.

That also explains why it's easy to miss. Pugh concedes the subversive potential isn't immediately apparent — and notes the franchise repeatedly stresses Link's place in the mythic hero tradition, with many scenes apparently endorsing the conventional storyline they're simultaneously undercutting.

sources.title: Minimalist Fiction in Six Short Stories

discussion.body: The withholding is the technique, not a side effect. If the prose explained the motive, there would be no story left, just a summary.
The nickname points the other way. “Kmart realism” is a claim about furniture and paychecks, not about syntax.
Both can hold at once: the compression is what lets the setting carry weight the narration refuses to state.

items.title: The Fiction That Got Nicknamed 'Kmart Realism'
items.body: Minimalist fiction is easy to caricature as short sentences and cold rooms. JSTOR Daily's description of the style is more useful than that: its language is direct, highly compressed and densely allusive, and much of what matters is left unstated. The reader has to decipher what a character actually wants, because motivation is inferred rather than explained out loud. That withholding is the whole engine of the form — a story that spells out the motive turns into a summary of itself. The subject matter helped give the style its joking name: minimalism is often associated with working-class characters, domestic life and marriages coming apart, a combination that earned it the nickname “Kmart realism.”

sources.title: Betting on the Midterms

items.title: What Two Betting Markets Say About the Midterms
items.body: Econbrowser reads the midterm odds off two prediction markets. On Polymarket, the sharp deterioration in Republican odds for holding the Senate occurred almost immediately after the beginning of the US-Iran War, and the first reversal between Republican and Democratic odds is dated to March 15. Kalshi put the odds of Democratic control of both houses at 59 percent. Two cautions come free with the numbers. Timing is not causation — a market can reprice for several reasons at once, and the start of a war is exactly the kind of moment when many things move together. And the two venues are not answering the same question: one is about the Senate majority, the other about both chambers.

sources.title: Alaska's salmon-feasting bears face off in biggest Fat Bear Week ever

items.title: A Bigger Bracket for Fat Bear Week
items.body: The bracket has grown. NPR reports this year's single-elimination tournament will have 16 competitors, compared to 12 in past years — a fuller field than the contest has run before. Alongside that, officials report more cubs in Katmai National Park than they've seen in recent memory. Sixteen adult contenders and an unusually crowded nursery: the park's season has been generous on both counts.

sources.title: Airport malaria in Germany remains infrequent

items.title: Malaria's Unlikely Stopover at Frankfurt Airport
items.body: An outbreak of malaria at Frankfurt Airport this summer raised alarm, DW reports, with experts believing the parasites probably arrived in a passenger's luggage. With the onset of fall, DW adds, the risk of contracting the disease is low. Two things are worth keeping separate here: the likely route the parasites took, which is a hypothesis attributed to experts, and the danger to anyone nearby, which is described as low and falling with the season.
